extracted.intended_audience: home cooks / household managers (19th-century domestic readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical household recipes and preservation methods for fruits, pickles, cordials, vinegars, beverages, and related household goods; gives ingredient ratios, processing times, and storage advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gooseberries — selection and stewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Select young gooseberries, make a syrup with one pound of loaf sugar to each of fruit; stew them till quite clear and the syrup becomes thick, but do not let them be mashed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cover the pan while they are stewing; keep fruit whole and avoid mashing to preserve appearance and texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apricots in brandy — fruit selection and syrup preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Take freshly gathered apricots not too ripe; to half their weight of loaf sugar, add as much water as will cover the fruit; boil and skim it: then put in the apricots, and let them remain five or six minutes: take them up without syrup, and lay them on dishes to cool; boil the syrup till reduced one half; when the apricots are cold, put them in bottles, and cover them with equal quantities of syrup and French brandy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the apricots be cling-stones, they will require more scalding; scald briefly in syrup, remove without excess syrup on fruit, and use equal parts syrup and brandy to cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peaches in brandy — cleaning and lye treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Get yellow soft peaches, perfectly free from defect and newly gathered, but not too ripe; place them in a pot, and cover them with cold weak lye; turn over those that float frequently... at the end of an hour take them out, wipe them carefully with a soft cloth to get off the down and skin, and lay them in cold water; make a syrup as for the apricots, and proceed in the same manner, only scald the peaches more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cold weak lye to remove down/skin; frequent turning ensures even action; scald longer than apricots; wipe carefully to avoid damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cherries in brandy — sugar proportion and ripeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the short stemmed bright red cherries in bunches--make a syrup, with equal quantities of sugar and cherries; scald the cherries, but do not let the skins crack, which they will do if the fruit be too ripe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose cherries not overripe to avoid skin-splitting; syrup ratio: equal weight sugar to cherries; scald enough to process but avoid bursting skins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plums in brandy — selection and sugar ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Select those that are free from blemish--make a syrup with half their weight of sugar, and preserve them in the same manner directed for apricots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unblemished fruit; syrup quantity: half the fruit's weight in sugar; follow the apricot-branding preservation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemon pickle — rind preparation and maceration
rubrics_metrics.description: Grate the yellow rind from two dozen fine fresh lemons, quarter them but leave them whole at the bottom; sprinkle salt on them, and put them in the sun every day until dry... pour on one gallon of strong vinegar, tie the pot close, put a board on, and let it stand three months--strain it, and when perfectly clear, bottle it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sun-dry with salt to desiccate rind; include specified spices (nutmegs, mace, horseradish, garlic, mustard seed); long maceration (3 months) then strain when perfectly clear before bottling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tomato catsup — concentration and seasonality
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather a peck of tomatos... put them on the fire without water, sprinkle on a few spoonsful of salt, let them boil steadily an hour, stirring them frequently; strain... put the liquid on the fire with half a pint of chopped onions, half a quarter of an ounce of mace... one table-spoonful of whole black pepper; boil all together until just enough to fill two bottles; cork it tight. Make it in August, in dry weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not add water when cooking tomatoes; frequent stirring; season and reduce to fill bottles; make during dry August weather for best results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tomato marmalade — use of green tomatoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather full grown tomatos while quite green; take out the stems, and stew them till soft; rub them through a sieve, put the pulp on the fire seasoned highly with pepper, salt, and pounded cloves; add some garlic, and stew all together till thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use green, full-grown tomatoes; heavy seasoning (pepper, salt, cloves, garlic) and long stewing to achieve thick marmalade for seasoning gravies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tomato sweet marmalade — sugar and gelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare it in the same manner, mix some loaf sugar with the pulp, and stew until it is a stiff jelly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add loaf sugar to pulp and cook to a stiff jelly consistency for sweet marmalade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tomato soy — salting, prolonged boiling, and spice mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a bushel of full ripe tomatos, cut them in slices without skinning--sprinkle the bottom of a large tub with salt, strew in the tomatos, and over each layer of about two inches thick, sprinkle half a pint of salt, and three onions sliced without taking off the skins. ... let them remain for three days, then put them into a large iron pot, in which they must boil from early in the morning till night, constantly stirring to prevent their sticking and mashing them. ... pass the mixture through a sieve, pressing it to obtain all the liquor you can; and add to it one ounce of cloves, quarter of a pound of allspice, quarter of a pound of whole black pepper, and a small wine glass of Cayenne; let it boil slowly and constantly during the whole of the day... Should it ferment it must be boiled a second time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salting in layers for 3 days to draw moisture; extremely long, slow boiling with constant stirring to concentrate without mashing; specified spice proportions; cool and bottle; store cool; if fermentation occurs, re-boil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pepper vinegar — concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Get one dozen pods of pepper when ripe, take out the stems, and cut them in two; put them in a kettle with three pints of vinegar, boil it away to one quart, and strain it through a sieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce vinegar volume by boiling to concentrate pepper flavor; strain and use as a flavoring in gravies and catsups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mushroom catsup — crushing, boiling, and reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the flaps of the proper mushrooms from the stems--wash them, add some salt, and crush them; then boil them some time, strain them through a cloth, put them on the fire again with salt to your taste, a few cloves of garlic, and a quarter of an ounce of cloves pounded, to a peck of mushrooms; boil it till reduced to less than half the original quantity--bottle and cork it well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crush and boil to extract flavor, strain through cloth, reboil with spices and reduce sharply; bottle and cork tightly for preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tarragon (astragon) vinegar — maceration timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick the tarragon nicely from the stem, let it lie in a dry place forty-eight hours; put it in a pitcher, and to one quart of the leaves put three pints of strong vinegar; cover it close, and let it stand a week--then strain it, and after standing in the pitcher till quite clear, bottle it, and cork it closely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dry tarragon 48 hours before maceration; use 1:3 leaves to vinegar ratio; macerate one week, then let liquid clear before bottling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curry powder — precise proportions and grinding
rubrics_metrics.description: One ounce turmeric, one do. coriander seed, one do. cummin seed, one do. white ginger, one of nutmeg, one of mace, and one of Cayenne pepper; pound all together, and pass them through a fine sieve; bottle and cork it well--one tea-spoonful is sufficient to season any made dish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal ounce proportions of listed spices; pound and sieve to fine powder; store in bottle; use sparingly (1 tsp per dish).

rubrics_metrics.name: To pickle cucumbers — brining, draining, and oil
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather them full grown, but quite young--take off the green rind, and slice them tolerably thick; put a layer in a deep dish, strew over it some chopped onion and salt; do this until they are all in; sprinkle salt on the top, let them stand six hours, put them in a colander--when all the liquor has run off, put them in a pot; strew a little cayenne pepper over each layer, and cover them with strong cold vinegar; when the pot is full, pour on some sweet oil, and tie it, up close; at the end of a fortnight, pour off the first vinegar, and put on fresh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial salting and draining (~6 hours) to draw moisture; use strong cold vinegar and cayenne between layers; add sweet oil on top and change vinegar after two weeks for best preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oil mangos (melons) — brine, seed removal and stuffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather the melons a size larger than a goose egg--put them in a pot, pour boiling salt and water made strong upon them, and cover them up; next day, cut a slit from the stem to the blossom end, and take out the seeds carefully--return them to the brine, and let them remain in it eight days; then put them in strong vinegar for a fortnight, wipe the insides with a soft cloth, stuff them and tie them, pack them in a pot with the slit uppermost; strew some of the stuffing over each layer, and keep them covered with the best vinegar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial hot brine, then seed removal and extended brining (8 days); follow with fortnight in strong vinegar; stuff and pack slit-side up; keep fully covered with good vinegar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stuffing for melons — ingredient proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wash a pound of white race ginger very clean; pour boiling water on it, and let it stand twenty-four hours; slice it thin, and dry it; one pound of horse-radish scraped and dried, one pound of mustard seed washed and dried, one pound of chopped onion, one ounce of mace, one of nutmeg pounded fine, two ounces of turmeric, and a handful of whole black pepper; make these ingredients into a paste, with a quarter of a pound of mustard, and a large cup full of sweet oil; put a clove of garlic into each mango.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed spice and herb proportions to make a paste stuffing; include one clove garlic per melon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yellow pickle — drying in sun and turmeric handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Put all the articles intended for the yellow pickle in a pot, and pour on them boiling salt and water--let them stand forty-eight hours, take advantage of a clear hot day, press the water from the articles, and lay them to dry in full sunshine... When dried, put them in a pot of plain cold vinegar, with a little turmeric in it--let them remain in it two weeks to draw off the water from them, and to make them plump--then put them in a clean pot, and pour on the vinegar, prepared by the following directions--mix the turmeric very smoothly, before you add it to your pickles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use boiling salt water to begin, stand 48 hours, then sun-dry on cloth to whiten and absorb moisture; initial soak in plain cold vinegar with some turmeric for two weeks to plump and draw off water; ensure turmeric is mixed smoothly to avoid spotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green pickles — repeated scalding to set color
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the articles you intend to pickle, in a pot--and cover them with boiling salt and water: put a thick cloth on the top, and then a plate that will fit it--let it stand till the next morning, then pour off the salt and water, boil it again, and cover them as before; do this until your pickles are a good green--then put them in plain cold vinegar, with some turmeric in it; and at the end of a fortnight, put them up, as you do the yellow pickle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated brief scalding and steaming under a cloth and plate over several days to fix green color; then treat like yellow pickles with cold vinegar and turmeric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepared vinegar for pickles — long maceration and reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: One pound of ginger sliced and dried, one of horse-radish scraped and dried, one of mustard seed washed and dried, one ounce long pepper, an ounce of mace, and one of nutmegs finely pounded; put all these ingredients in a pot, pour two gallons of strong vinegar on, and let it stand twelve months, stirring it very frequently. When this vinegar is used for the pickles, put two gallons more vinegar, with some mace and nutmegs, and keep it for another year. ... Pickles keep much better when the vinegar is not boiled. Should the green pickles at any time lose their colour, it may be restored by adding a little more turmeric. All pickles are best, when one or two years old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare spiced vinegar by macerating spices for 12 months with frequent stirring; replenish and age further; avoid boiling vinegar for pickles; turmeric can restore color; allow pickles to mature 1–2 years for best keeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickle vessels — material and shape
rubrics_metrics.description: The vessels for keeping pickles should be made of stone ware, straight from the bottom to the top, with stone covers to them; when the mouth is very wide, the pickles may be taken out without breaking them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use straight-sided stoneware with stone covers to minimize breakage and allow easy removal; material selection affects preservation quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onions — brining regimen and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Get white onions that are not too large, cut the stem close to the root with a sharp knife, put them in a pot, pour on boiling salt and water to cover them, stop the pot closely, let them stand a fortnight, changing the salt and water every three days; they must be stirred daily, or those that float will become soft; at the end of this time, take off the skin and outer shell, put them in plain cold vinegar with a little turmeric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extended hot brine (2 weeks) with periodic changes every 3 days and daily stirring to prevent softening; final storage in cold vinegar with turmeric for color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nasturtiums (berries) — short brine then vinegar
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather the berries when full grown but young, put them in a pot, pour boiling salt and water on, and let them stand three or four days; then drain off the water, and cover them with cold vinegar; add a few blades of mace, and whole grains of black pepper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short hot brine 3–4 days then transfer to cold vinegar with mace and whole pepper to flavor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radish pods — steaming to set green color and oil/turmeric trick
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut them in nice bunches as soon as they are fully formed; they must be young and tender--pour boiling salt and water on them, cover with a thick cloth, and pewter plate, to keep in the steam; repeat this every day till they are a good green; then put them in cold vinegar, with mace and whole pepper; mix a little turmeric, with a small portion of oil, and stir it into the vinegar; it will make the pods of a more lively green.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use steam-trapping (cloth and plate) daily to set bright green; add turmeric mixed with oil into vinegar to enhance color for garnishing meats.

rubrics_metrics.name: English walnuts — harvest timing and brining schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The walnuts should be gathered when the nut is so young that you can run a pin into it easily; pour boiling salt and water on, and let them be covered with it nine days, changing it every third day--take them out, and put them on dishes in the air for a few minutes, taking care to turn them over; this will make them black much sooner--put them in a pot, strew over some whole pepper, cloves, a little garlic, mustard seed, and horse-radish scraped and dried; cover them with strong cold vinegar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harvest extremely young nuts; hot brine for 9 days with changes every 3 days; brief air exposure hastens darkening; pack with spices and strong cold vinegar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peppers (bell) — long brine and vein caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather the large bell pepper when quite young, leave the seeds in and the stem on, cut a slit in one side between the large veins, to let the water in; pour boiling salt and water on, changing it every day for three weeks--you must keep them closely stopped; if at the end of this time, they be a good green, put them in pots, and cover them with cold vinegar and a little turmeric; those that are not sufficiently green, must be continued under the same process till they are so. Be careful not to cut through the large veins, as the heat will instantly diffuse itself through the pod.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extended hot brining (up to 3 weeks with daily changes) while keeping sealed; slit only between large veins to let brine in, avoid cutting veins to prevent whole-pod overheating; finish in cold vinegar with turmeric when color set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walnut catsup — maceration and spicing
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather the walnuts as for pickling, and keep them in salt and water the same time; then pound them in a marble mortar--to every dozen walnuts, put a quart of vinegar; stir them well every day for a week, then put them in a bag, and press all the liquor through; to each quart, put a tea-spoonful of pounded cloves, and one of mace, with six cloves of garlic--boil it fifteen or twenty minutes, and bottle it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macerate walnut pulp in vinegar with daily stirring for a week; press to extract liquor; add specified spices; boil 15–20 minutes before bottling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green nectarines/apricots — green them and two-week vinegar soak
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather them while the shell is soft--green them with salt and water as before directed; when a good green, soak them in plain vinegar for a fortnight, and put them in the yellow pickle pot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harvest while shell still soft; use salting/greening regimen and then fortnight in plain vinegar prior to final pickling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asparagus — quick brine then yellow pickle
rubrics_metrics.description: Pour boiling salt and water on, and cover them close--next day, take them out, dry them, and after standing in vinegar, put them with the yellow pickle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short hot brine followed by drying and standing in vinegar before combining with yellow pickle batch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ginger wine — proportions and fermentation timing
rubrics_metrics.description: To three gallons of water, put three pounds of sugar, and four ounces of race ginger, washed in many waters to cleanse it; boil them together for one hour, and strain it through a sieve; when lukewarm, put it in a cask with three lemons cut in slices, and two gills of beer yeast; shake it well, and stop the cask very tight; let it stand a week to ferment; and if not clear enough to bottle, it must remain until it becomes so; it will be fit to drink in ten days after bottling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specified sugar:water:ginger proportions; one hour boiling; ferment with beer yeast in cask ~1 week then longer until clear; bottle when clear and wait ~10 days after bottling to drink.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orgeat — milk blanching and almond processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Boil two quarts of milk with a stick of cinnamon and let it stand to be quite cold, first taking out the cinnamon; blanch four ounces of the best sweet almonds, pound them in a marble mortar with a little rose-water; mix them well with the milk, sweeten it to your taste, and let it boil a few minutes only, lest the almonds should be oily; strain it through a very fine sieve till quite smooth, and free from the almonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief boiling after combining to avoid oiliness from almonds; strain finely to remove almond residue; serve cold or lukewarm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cherry shrub — juice extraction and brandy addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather ripe morello cherries, pick them from the stalk, and put them in an earthen pot, which must be set into an iron pot of water; make the water boil, but take care that none of it gets into the cherries; when the juice is extracted, pour it into a bag made of tolerably thick cloth... sweeten it to your taste, and when it becomes perfectly clear, bottle it--put a gill of brandy into each bottle, before you pour in the juice--cover the corks with rosin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gentle steam-heat (double-pot) to extract juice without water contact; press through cloth; sweeten and wait for clarity; add brandy to each bottle and seal corks with rosin for storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currant wine — fruit:rack sugar:water ratios and clearing times
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather full ripe currants on a dry day, pick them from the stalks, and weigh them; then crush them with your hands, leaving none whole; for every two pounds of currants put one quart of water... then, for every three pounds of currants, put one pound of powdered loaf sugar; ... let it stand sixteen hours to cool, before you put it in the cask--stop it very close. If the quantity be twenty gallons, let it stand three weeks before you bottle it; if it be thirty gallons, it must remain a month; it should be perfectly clear when drawn off--put a lump of sugar in each bottle, cork it well, and keep it in a cool place, or it will turn sour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow precise fruit:water and fruit:sugar ratios; allow cooling, fermenting and clearing times proportional to batch size (3 weeks for 20 gal, 1 month for 30 gal); bottle only when perfectly clear and store cool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping lemon-juice — sugar, brandy and sealing
rubrics_metrics.description: Get lemons quite free from blemish, squeeze them, and strain the juice; to each pint of it, put a pound of good loaf sugar pounded; stir it frequently until the sugar is completely dissolved, cover the pitcher closely, and let it stand till the dregs have subsided, and the syrup is transparent; have bottles perfectly clean and dry, put a wine glass full of French brandy into each bottle, fill it with syrup, cork it, and dip the neck into melted rosin or pitch; keep them in a cool dry cellar--do not put it on the fire--it will destroy the fine flavour of the juice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 1 lb sugar per pint juice, add ~1 wine glass French brandy per bottle, ensure cleanliness and dryness of bottles, seal necks in rosin/pitch, store cool/dry, and do not heat the juice or syrup (heating ruins flavor).

rubrics_metrics.name: To make soap — lye strength test and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Put on the fire any quantity of lye you choose that is strong enough to bear an egg--to each gallon, add three quarters of a pound of clean grease: boil it very fast, and stir it frequently--a few hours will suffice to make it good soap. ... When you find by cooling a little on a plate that it is a thick jelly, and no grease appears, put in salt in the proportion of one pint to three gallons... Next day, cut out the soap, melt it, and cool it again; this takes out all the lye, and keeps the soap from shrinking when dried. ... Soft soap is made in the same manner, only omitting the salt. ... Kitchen grease should be clarified in a quantity of water, or the salt will prevent its incorporating with the lye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test lye by floating an egg; standard ratio: 3/4 lb grease per gallon lye; boil fast and stir for hours; check plate-cool for 'thick jelly' before adding salt (1 pint salt : 3 gallons); remelt next day to remove excess lye; clarify kitchen grease first; optional sun method: mix and place in sun 8–10 days stirring several times daily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying herbs — harvest timing and storage
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather them on a dry day, just before they begin to blossom; brush off the dust, cut them in small branches, and dry them quickly in a moderate oven; pick off the leaves when dry, pound and sift them--bottle them immediately, and cork them closely. They must be kept in a dry place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harvest just before blooming on a dry day; dry quickly in moderate oven; store immediately in sealed bottles in a dry location to preserve flavor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning silver — alum and lye mixture
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissolve two tea-spoonsful of alum in a quart of moderately strong lye--stir in a gill of soft soap, and skim off the dross. Wash the silver clean in hot water, let it remain covered with this mixture for ten or fifteen minutes, turning it over frequently; then wash it in hot soap suds, and rub it well with a dry cloth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare alum + lye + soft soap mixture; immerse and turn silver for 10–15 minutes; follow with hot soap suds and dry rub. Use caution with lye strength and rinsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning knives and forks — avoid very hot water
rubrics_metrics.description: Wash them in warm water, and wipe them till quite dry; then touch them lightly over, without smearing the handles, with rotten stone made wet; let it dry on them, and then rub with a clean cloth... must never be put into very hot water, lest the handles be injured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use warm (not very hot) water to preserve handles; use rotten stone sparingly on metal and polish dry; frequent steel use keeps edge sharp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blacking — composition and boiling porter medium
rubrics_metrics.description: A quarter of a pound of ivory black, two ounces of sugar candy, a quarter of an ounce of gum tragacanth; pound them all very fine, boil a bottle of porter, and stir the ingredients in while boiling hot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine powdered materials finely and incorporate into boiling porter to make blacking; bottle/mediate proportions specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aromatic & medicinal waters — recipes and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Lavender water: Put a pint of highly rectified spirits of wine, to one ounce of essential oil of lavender, and two drachms of ambergris; shake them well together, and keep it closely stopped. Hungarian water: One pint spirits of wine, one ounce oil of rosemary, and two drachms essence of ambergris. Cologne water: Three quarts spirits of wine, six drachms oil of lavender, one drachm oil of rosemary, three drachms essence of lemon, ten drops oil of cinnamon--mix them together very well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise spirit:oil:essence ratios for perfumed waters; mix thoroughly and store sealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vinegar of the Four Thieves — herb maceration in sun
rubrics_metrics.description: Take lavender, rosemary, sage, wormwood, rue, and mint, of each a large handful; put them in a pot of earthen ware, pour on them four quarts of very strong vinegar, cover the pot closely, and put a board on the top; keep it in the hottest sun two weeks, then strain and bottle it, putting in each bottle a clove of garlic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make when herbs are in full vigour (June); sun-macerate herbs two weeks in strong vinegar; strain repeatedly until clear; add clove garlic to bottles; use as refreshing/vaporizing vinegar in rooms and sick apartments.
